1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 b6 4.g3 Bb7.name: Queen's Indian Defence: Fianchetto Variation, Traditional Line
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 b6 4.g3 Bb7.background: The standard reply to 4.g3 through the 1970s, and the most frequently played line from the 1950s until 4...Ba6 became popular in the 1980s.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 b6 4.g3 Bb7 5.Bg2.strategy: Completes the fianchetto: the bishop supports d5 and e4 and will rake the long diagonal once the knight on f3 has moved. It also clears the way to castle, so White gets a safe king and slow, lasting pressure on the centre.

A simple developing move: Black prepares to castle, keeps e4 and d5 under watch and waits for White to commit. White gets more space, Black a solid position with few weaknesses, and a long manoeuvring game in which Black has real chances to equalise.

Aims to trade Black's less useful dark-squared bishop for a white piece. It is solid, but White interposes easily, and Black's pieces end up with little scope, so the bishop's exchange leaves Black slightly passive.

Strikes at d4 before either side has castled, trading a solid development for early central play. If White closes the centre or captures, the structure changes and Black's bishop on b7 depends on a pawn break to come alive; it is a double-edged choice.
